1. Strongly continuous (C₀) semigroups

A linear autonomous evolution equation $u'(t)=Au(t)$, $u(0)=u_0$, on a Banach space $X$ should have a solution operator: take initial data, return the state at time $t$. Encode the family of such operators as a map $T\colon[0,\infty)\to B(X)$ satisfying three properties:

  • $T(0)=I$ (zero time, no evolution);
  • $T(s+t)=T(s)\,T(t)$ for $s,t\ge 0$ (Chapman–Kolmogorov / time-translation invariance);
  • $t\mapsto T(t)x$ is continuous in $t$ for every fixed $x\in X$ (the strong-continuity axiom).

Such a family $\{T(t)\}_{t\ge 0}$ is a strongly continuous semigroup, or $C_0$-semigroup. The third axiom is the weakest reasonable one: norm continuity ($\|T(t)-T(s)\|\to 0$) is far too strong — it forces the generator to be bounded, ruling out most PDE examples. Pointwise-in-$x$ continuity is the right calibration: differential operators have $T(t)\to I$ strongly but never in operator norm.

The structural growth bound is automatic: there exist $M\ge 1$ and $\omega\in\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$\|T(t)\|_{B(X)} \;\le\; M\,e^{\omega t} \qquad \text{for all } t\ge 0.$$

The proof is short: strong continuity at $t=0$ plus the uniform-boundedness principle gives $\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\|T(t)\|\le M$, then the semigroup law extends this to every $t$ by writing $t=n+s$. The constants $(M,\omega)$ classify the semigroup: $\omega\le 0$ with $M=1$ is the contraction case, $\omega=0$ alone is uniformly bounded, and the infimum of admissible $\omega$ is the growth bound $\omega_0(T)$.

Three canonical PDE examples set the picture. The heat semigroup $T(t)=e^{t\Delta}$ on $X=L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a contraction: $\|T(t)f\|_{L^2}\le\|f\|_{L^2}$ by Plancherel applied to the Fourier multiplier $e^{-t|\xi|^2}$, which has modulus $\le 1$. The wave-equation propagator on $X=H^1\times L^2$ (the energy space, holding $(u,u_t)$) is a $C_0$-group, $\|T(t)\|\le 1$ in the energy norm, signed time. The Schrödinger group $T(t)=e^{-it\Delta}$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a unitary $C_0$-group: $\|T(t)f\|_{L^2}=\|f\|_{L^2}$ exactly, and reversibility means we can run time backwards.

<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.getElementById('sg-c0-svg');
  const out = document.getElementById('sg-c0-out');
  const tS = document.getElementById('sg-c0-t');
  const sS = document.getElementById('sg-c0-s');
  const tO = document.getElementById('sg-c0-t-out');
  const sO = document.getElementById('sg-c0-s-out');
  const bH = document.getElementById('sg-c0-heat');
  const bW = document.getElementById('sg-c0-wave');
  const bQ = document.getElementById('sg-c0-schro');
  let kind = 'heat';
  function setH(){ kind='heat'; bH.classList.add('active'); bW.classList.remove('active'); bQ.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  function setW(){ kind='wave'; bW.classList.add('active'); bH.classList.remove('active'); bQ.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  function setQ(){ kind='schro'; bQ.classList.add('active'); bH.classList.remove('active'); bW.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  const N = 120;
  const xs = [];
  for(let k=0;k<N;k++) xs.push(-Math.PI + (2*Math.PI*k)/(N-1));
  function u0(x){ return Math.exp(-3*x*x); }
  // Direct evaluation T(t) u0 by closed form (heat: Gaussian widening with operator Delta; wave: d'Alembert; Schrodinger: e^{itDelta} on Gaussian, denominator 1+4iat, a=3 so 1+12it).
  function applyT(t){
    if(kind === 'heat'){
      const sigma2 = 1/6 + 2*t;
      const amp = Math.sqrt((1/6)/sigma2);
      return xs.map(x => amp * Math.exp(-x*x/(2*sigma2)));
    }
    if(kind === 'wave'){
      return xs.map(x => 0.5*(u0(x-t) + u0(x+t)));
    }
    const a = 3;
    return xs.map(x => {
      const rD = 1, iD = 4*a*t;
      const mod2 = rD*rD + iD*iD;
      const invR = rD/mod2, invI = -iD/mod2;
      const re = -a*x*x*invR, im = -a*x*x*invI;
      const expR = Math.exp(re);
      const cosI = Math.cos(im), sinI = Math.sin(im);
      const ampSqrt = Math.pow(mod2, 0.25);
      const phaseSqrt = 0.5 * Math.atan2(iD, rD);
      const uR = (expR*cosI*Math.cos(-phaseSqrt) - expR*sinI*Math.sin(-phaseSqrt)) / ampSqrt;
      return uR;
    });
  }
  // Composed evaluation T(s) o T(t) u0 by numerical kernel convolution / shift / mode propagation.
  // Heat: convolve current state with Gaussian kernel of variance 2s. Wave: shift current state +- s and average. Schrodinger: discrete Fourier coefficients then phase k^2 s.
  function applyTcomposed(t, s){
    const utArr = applyT(t);
    if(kind === 'wave'){
      // d'Alembert: T(s) on already-evolved state advances each traveling wave by s; for our explicit u0, T(s)(T(t)u0)(x) = 1/2[u0(x-(t+s)) + u0(x+(t+s))] - we synthesize that by sampling u_t shifted +/- s.
      const arr = new Array(xs.length).fill(0);
      for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
        const x = xs[k];
        // Linear interpolation of utArr at x +- s
        function interp(y){
          const j0 = (y - xs[0]) / (xs[1]-xs[0]);
          const j = Math.max(0, Math.min(xs.length-2, Math.floor(j0)));
          const a = j0 - j;
          return utArr[j]*(1-a) + utArr[j+1]*a;
        }
        arr[k] = 0.5*(interp(x-s) + interp(x+s));
      }
      return arr;
    }
    if(kind === 'heat'){
      // Discrete heat kernel convolution with variance 2s
      if(s < 1e-6) return utArr.slice();
      const arr = new Array(xs.length).fill(0);
      const sigma = Math.sqrt(2*s);
      const half = Math.min(4*sigma, Math.PI);
      const M = 60;
      for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
        const x = xs[k];
        let acc = 0, norm = 0;
        for(let j=0;j<=M;j++){
          const y = -half + (2*half*j)/M;
          const w = Math.exp(-(y*y)/(4*s));
          // sample utArr at x - y
          const j0 = (x - y - xs[0]) / (xs[1]-xs[0]);
          const ji = Math.max(0, Math.min(xs.length-2, Math.floor(j0)));
          const aa = j0 - ji;
          const v = utArr[ji]*(1-aa) + utArr[ji+1]*aa;
          acc += v * w; norm += w;
        }
        arr[k] = acc/norm;
      }
      return arr;
    }
    // Schrodinger: take DFT of utArr (real), apply phase e^{i k^2 s} per mode, inverse-DFT real part.
    const K = 32;
    const ck = [];
    for(let kk=-K;kk<=K;kk++){
      let re = 0, im = 0;
      for(let j=0;j<xs.length-1;j++){
        const xj = xs[j];
        re += utArr[j] * Math.cos(kk*xj);
        im -= utArr[j] * Math.sin(kk*xj);
      }
      ck.push({k:kk, re: re/(xs.length-1), im: im/(xs.length-1)});
    }
    return xs.map(x => {
      let acc = 0;
      for(const {k:kk, re, im} of ck){
        const phase = kk*kk * s;
        const c = Math.cos(phase), si = Math.sin(phase);
        const newR = re*c - im*si;
        const newI = re*si + im*c;
        acc += newR * Math.cos(kk*x) - newI * Math.sin(kk*x);
      }
      return acc;
    });
  }
  function clamp01(v){ return Math.max(-1.4, Math.min(1.4, v)); }
  function draw(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const t = +tS.value, s = +sS.value;
    tO.textContent = `t = ${t.toFixed(2)}`;
    sO.textContent = `s = ${s.toFixed(2)}`;
    const xL = -240, xR = 240, yMid = 0;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL,y1:yMid,x2:xR,y2:yMid,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:0,y1:-120,x2:0,y2:120,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6,'stroke-dasharray':'2 3'}));
    const X = x => x * (220/Math.PI);
    const Y = v => -clamp01(v) * 70;
    function plot(arr, color, dash, width){
      let d = '';
      for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
        const px = X(xs[k]), py = Y(arr[k]);
        d += (k===0 ? 'M' : 'L') + ` ${px.toFixed(1)} ${py.toFixed(1)} `;
      }
      const p = SVG('path',{d, fill:'none', stroke:color, 'stroke-width':width||1.6});
      if(dash) p.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', dash);
      svg.appendChild(p);
    }
    plot(applyT(0), 'var(--mute)', '4 3');
    plot(applyT(t), 'var(--cyan)', null);
    const Tst = applyT(s+t);
    plot(Tst, 'var(--yellow)', null, 2.4);
    const Tcomp = applyTcomposed(t, s);
    plot(Tcomp, 'var(--violet)', '3 2', 1.4);
    let maxDiff = 0;
    for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
      maxDiff = Math.max(maxDiff, Math.abs(Tst[k] - Tcomp[k]));
    }
    for(let m=-3; m<=3; m++){
      const px = X(m);
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:px,y1:yMid-3,x2:px,y2:yMid+3,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
    }
    const lg = (x, y, c, txt, dash) => {
      const ln = SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:y,x2:x+18,y2:y,stroke:c,'stroke-width':2});
      if(dash) ln.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', dash);
      svg.appendChild(ln);
      const tt = SVG('text',{x:x+24,y:y+3,'font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      tt.textContent = txt; svg.appendChild(tt);
    };
    lg(-235, -130, 'var(--mute)', 'u0', '4 3');
    lg(-205, -118, 'var(--cyan)', 'T(t) u0');
    lg(-145, -130, 'var(--yellow)', 'T(s+t) u0 (direct)');
    lg(-25, -130, 'var(--violet)', 'T(s)·T(t) u0 (composed)', '3 2');
    const sumLabel = SVG('text',{x:0, y:130, 'text-anchor':'middle', 'font-size':11, fill:'var(--ink)'});
    const desc = kind === 'heat'
      ? `Heat semigroup: u0=e^{-3x^2} stays Gaussian; T(t) widens variance by 2t. Composing T(s)T(t) widens by 2s+2t = 2(s+t), matching T(s+t).`
      : kind === 'wave'
      ? `Wave 1D, c=1, u_t(0)=0: d'Alembert gives 1/2(u0(x-t)+u0(x+t)). Two pulses split; T(s) on each adds another shift, equivalent to running the original time t+s.`
      : `Schroedinger free particle: phase-modulated Gaussian; |T(t)u0|_{L^2} stays equal to |u0|_{L^2} (unitary). T(s)T(t) = T(s+t) by linearity of the free Hamiltonian phase.`;
    sumLabel.textContent = desc;
    svg.appendChild(sumLabel);
    const xAxisL = SVG('text',{x:230,y:14,'text-anchor':'end','font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
    xAxisL.textContent = 'x'; svg.appendChild(xAxisL);
    out.textContent = `Semigroup: ${kind === 'heat' ? 'heat (parabolic, contraction)' : kind === 'wave' ? 'wave (hyperbolic, isometric group)' : 'Schroedinger (dispersive, unitary group)'}    s = ${s.toFixed(2)}, t = ${t.toFixed(2)}, s+t = ${(s+t).toFixed(2)}.
Direct path T(s+t) u0 (yellow) and composed path T(s)·(T(t) u0) (violet, dashed) overlay; max pointwise difference approx ${maxDiff.toExponential(2)} (numerical / discretization noise; converges to 0 with finer grids). This IS the semigroup law made visible.
Growth bound: |T(t)| <= 1 in all three cases shown (M=1, omega=0). Heat is a contraction, wave/Schroedinger are isometries.`;
  }
  bH.addEventListener('click', setH);
  bW.addEventListener('click', setW);
  bQ.addEventListener('click', setQ);
  tS.addEventListener('input', draw);
  sS.addEventListener('input', draw);
  draw();
})();
</script>

2. The infinitesimal generator

The whole semigroup is encoded by its behavior at $t=0^+$. Given a $C_0$-semigroup $T(t)$ on $X$, define the infinitesimal generator $A$ by

$$Ax \;=\; \lim_{t\to 0^+}\frac{T(t)x - x}{t},\qquad D(A) \;=\; \Bigl\{x\in X \;:\; \text{this limit exists in }X\Bigr\}.$$

The basic structure of $A$ is forced by the semigroup axioms:

  • $D(A)$ is a dense linear subspace of $X$ (density follows from $\frac{1}{t}\int_0^t T(s)x\,ds\to x$ and the integrals lie in $D(A)$);
  • $A$ is closed: $\{(x_n,Ax_n)\}\to (x,y)$ in $X\times X$ forces $x\in D(A)$ and $Ax=y$;
  • $A$ is uniquely determined by $T$, and conversely $T$ is uniquely determined by $A$ — the generator is a complete invariant.

The fundamental differentiation identity is the operator analogue of $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}T(t)x \;=\; A\,T(t)x \;=\; T(t)\,A x \qquad \text{for }x\in D(A),\ t\ge 0.$$

So orbits starting in $D(A)$ are differentiable, and $u(t)=T(t)u_0$ is a classical solution of $u'=Au$, $u(0)=u_0$. For $u_0\in X\setminus D(A)$ the orbit need not be differentiable but is still continuous; we call $T(t)u_0$ a mild solution (the integrated form of the equation). The generator $A$ is bounded ($A\in B(X)$) iff $T$ is uniformly continuous, and in that case $T(t)=e^{tA}=\sum_{k\ge 0}(tA)^k/k!$ converges in operator norm.

Examples make the rough/smooth distinction concrete. For the heat semigroup on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $A=\Delta$ with $D(A)=H^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ — two derivatives in $L^2$. For the translation semigroup $T(t)f(x)=f(x+t)$ on $L^p(\mathbb{R})$, $A=d/dx$ with $D(A)=W^{1,p}$. The pattern is that $D(A)$ is the natural Sobolev space the differential operator $A$ likes; functions outside $D(A)$ don't have enough regularity for the strong limit to converge.

3. The Hille–Yosida theorem

Which closed densely-defined operators $A$ are generators of $C_0$-semigroups? The full classification is the Hille–Yosida theorem (Hille 1948, Yosida 1948 — independent proofs). Stated for contractions ($M=1$, $\omega=0$):

$A$ generates a $C_0$-semigroup of contractions iff $A$ is closed, densely defined, every $\lambda>0$ lies in the resolvent set $\rho(A)$, and

$$\bigl\|\,(\lambda I - A)^{-1}\,\bigr\|_{B(X)} \;\le\; \frac{1}{\lambda} \qquad \text{for all }\lambda>0.$$

The extension to general $C_0$-semigroups with $\|T(t)\|\le M e^{\omega t}$ requires the resolvent estimate at every $\lambda>\omega$ on every iterate: $\|(\lambda-A)^{-n}\|\le M/(\lambda-\omega)^n$ for $n=1,2,\ldots$. The single-power estimate suffices only for $M=1$.

The Lumer–Phillips theorem repackages this without the iterate condition. Call $A$ dissipative if $\|(\lambda - A)x\|\ge\lambda\|x\|$ for every $\lambda>0$ and $x\in D(A)$ (equivalently, on a Hilbert space, $\mathrm{Re}\langle Ax,x\rangle\le 0$). Lumer–Phillips: $A$ generates a contraction $C_0$-semigroup iff $A$ is dissipative and $\mathrm{range}(\lambda - A) = X$ for some (equivalently, every) $\lambda>0$. The range condition is the hard hypothesis to check; on a Hilbert space it follows from $A$ closed plus $A^*$ also dissipative.

The proof of the existence direction is the Yosida approximation: define

$$A_n \;=\; n\,A\,(n - A)^{-1} \;=\; n^2(n-A)^{-1} - n\,I,$$

which is a bounded operator on $X$ (the resolvent estimate guarantees $\|n(n-A)^{-1}\|\le 1$). Then $A_n x\to Ax$ for $x\in D(A)$, the bounded exponential $T_n(t)=e^{tA_n}=\sum_k(tA_n)^k/k!$ is well-defined for each $n$, and $T_n(t)\to T(t)$ strongly. The Yosida approximation is the operator-theoretic analogue of regularizing an unbounded function by a bounded approximant: trade strong convergence away from a singularity for the right to compute classical exponentials on the regularization.

<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.getElementById('sg-hy-svg');
  const out = document.getElementById('sg-hy-out');
  const lS = document.getElementById('sg-hy-l');
  const lO = document.getElementById('sg-hy-l-out');
  const bD = document.getElementById('sg-hy-diss');
  const bB = document.getElementById('sg-hy-bad');
  let kind = 'diss';
  function setD(){ kind='diss'; bD.classList.add('active'); bB.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  function setB(){ kind='bad'; bB.classList.add('active'); bD.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  const N = 240;
  const xs = [];
  for(let k=0;k<N;k++) xs.push(-Math.PI + (2*Math.PI*k)/(N-1));
  // Smooth periodic test function: avoids Gibbs at +-pi (sin(3x) - 0.5 sin(7x) is exactly 2pi-periodic)
  function f(x){ return Math.sin(3*x) - 0.5*Math.sin(7*x); }
  function resolvent(lambda){
    if(kind === 'bad'){
      const denom = lambda - 1.0;
      if(Math.abs(denom) < 1e-3){
        return xs.map(_ => 1/1e-3 * 1.0);
      }
      return xs.map(x => f(x) / denom);
    }
    const K = 32;
    const ck = [];
    for(let k=-K;k<=K;k++){
      let re = 0, im = 0;
      for(let j=0;j<xs.length-1;j++){
        const xj = xs[j];
        re += f(xj) * Math.cos(k*xj);
        im -= f(xj) * Math.sin(k*xj);
      }
      ck.push({k, re: re/(xs.length-1), im: im/(xs.length-1)});
    }
    return xs.map(x => {
      let s = 0;
      for(const {k, re, im} of ck){
        const denom = lambda + k*k;
        const cR = re/denom, cI = im/denom;
        s += cR * Math.cos(k*x) - cI * Math.sin(k*x);
      }
      return s;
    });
  }
  function draw(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const lambda = +lS.value;
    lO.textContent = `lambda = ${lambda.toFixed(2)}`;
    const xL = -240, xR = 240;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL,y1:0,x2:xR,y2:0,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:0,y1:-120,x2:0,y2:120,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6,'stroke-dasharray':'2 3'}));
    const X = x => x * (220/Math.PI);
    const Y = v => -Math.max(-1.4, Math.min(1.4, v)) * 60;
    function plot(arr, color, dash){
      let d = '';
      for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
        const px = X(xs[k]), py = Y(arr[k]);
        d += (k===0 ? 'M' : 'L') + ` ${px.toFixed(1)} ${py.toFixed(1)} `;
      }
      const p = SVG('path',{d, fill:'none', stroke:color, 'stroke-width':1.6});
      if(dash) p.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', dash);
      svg.appendChild(p);
    }
    const fArr = xs.map(f);
    plot(fArr, 'var(--mute)', '3 3');
    const rArr = resolvent(lambda);
    plot(rArr, 'var(--cyan)', null);
    const yArr = rArr.map((v,i) => lambda*lambda*v - lambda*fArr[i]);
    plot(yArr, 'var(--violet)', '4 3');
    // Discrete L^2 norm ratio - the right norm for the operator-norm bound on a self-adjoint generator.
    let l2R = 0, l2F = 0;
    const dx = xs[1] - xs[0];
    for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){ l2R += rArr[k]*rArr[k]*dx; l2F += fArr[k]*fArr[k]*dx; }
    l2R = Math.sqrt(l2R); l2F = Math.sqrt(l2F);
    const ratio = l2R / Math.max(l2F, 1e-9);
    const bound = 1/lambda;
    const lg = (x, y, c, txt, dash) => {
      const ln = SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:y,x2:x+18,y2:y,stroke:c,'stroke-width':2});
      if(dash) ln.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', dash);
      svg.appendChild(ln);
      const t = SVG('text',{x:x+24,y:y+3,'font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent = txt; svg.appendChild(t);
    };
    lg(-235, -130, 'var(--mute)', 'f', '3 3');
    lg(-180, -130, 'var(--cyan)', '(lambda-A)^{-1} f');
    lg(-95, -130, 'var(--violet)', 'A_lambda f (Yosida)', '4 3');
    if(kind === 'diss'){
      out.textContent = `Dissipative A = d^2/dx^2 (periodic). Resolvent (lambda-A)^{-1} acts on a smooth periodic test function f = sin(3x) - 0.5 sin(7x); each Fourier mode is divided by (lambda+k^2).
At lambda = ${lambda.toFixed(2)}: |(lambda-A)^{-1} f|_{L^2} approx ${l2R.toFixed(3)}, |f|_{L^2} approx ${l2F.toFixed(3)}, L^2-ratio ${ratio.toFixed(3)} <= 1/lambda = ${bound.toFixed(3)} (Hille-Yosida bound holds; equality is reached as lambda goes to 0+ when the lowest mode dominates).
The Yosida approximant A_lambda = lambda^2 (lambda-A)^{-1} - lambda I is bounded; A_lambda f converges to Af = d^2 f /dx^2 = -9 sin(3x) + 24.5 sin(7x) as lambda goes to infinity.`;
    } else {
      const ratioBad = 1/Math.abs(lambda-1);
      const violated = ratioBad > bound + 1e-9;
      out.textContent = `Non-dissipative A = +1*I. Spectrum is {1}; resolvent (lambda-A)^{-1} = (lambda-1)^{-1} I, so its operator norm is exactly 1/|lambda-1|.
At lambda = ${lambda.toFixed(2)}: ||(lambda-A)^{-1}|| = ${ratioBad.toFixed(3)}; Hille-Yosida would require <= 1/lambda = ${bound.toFixed(3)}.
${violated ? 'Bound VIOLATED - A does NOT generate a contraction semigroup. (It does generate e^{tI} = e^t * I, a growing semigroup, but omega=1 not 0.)' : 'Bound holds at this lambda, but Hille-Yosida demands the bound for EVERY lambda > 0; slide near lambda = 1 (or above) to see the violation.'}
Lesson: dissipativity of A is necessary for contraction; otherwise the resolvent norm exceeds 1/lambda for some lambda > 0 and Hille-Yosida fails.`;
    }
  }

  bB.addEventListener('click', setB);
  lS.addEventListener('input', draw);
  draw();
})();

4. Analytic semigroups and parabolic regularity

The heat semigroup is sharper than a generic $C_0$-semigroup in two visible ways: $T(t)u_0$ is instantaneously $C^\infty$ for any $u_0\in L^2$, and $T(t)$ extends from $t\in[0,\infty)$ to a holomorphic family on a complex sector. These two facts are equivalent. A $C_0$-semigroup $T(t)$ on $X$ is analytic if there is a sector

$$\Sigma_\delta \;=\; \{\,z\in\mathbb{C}\,:\,z\ne 0,\ |\arg z|<\delta\,\},\qquad 0<\delta\le\pi/2,$$

and a holomorphic extension $T\colon \Sigma_\delta\to B(X)$ such that $T(t_1+t_2)=T(t_1)T(t_2)$ for $t_1,t_2\in\Sigma_\delta$ and $T(z)x\to x$ as $z\to 0$ in any subsector $\Sigma_{\delta'}$, $\delta'<\delta$.

The resolvent characterization is what one actually checks in practice. $A$ generates an analytic $C_0$-semigroup iff there is some $\delta\in(0,\pi/2]$ such that the resolvent set contains the sector $\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}:\lambda\ne 0,\ |\arg\lambda|<\pi/2+\delta\}$ and

$$\bigl\|\,(\lambda - A)^{-1}\,\bigr\| \;\le\; \frac{M}{|\lambda|}\qquad \text{on this sector.}$$

Compared to Hille–Yosida (which only needs $\lambda>0$), analyticity demands the resolvent estimate on a fattened half-plane that bulges past the imaginary axis. This is why second-order elliptic operators (Laplacian, more general uniformly elliptic $-\nabla\cdot(a\nabla)$) generate analytic semigroups but first-order skew-symmetric operators (like $i\,d/dx$ for Schrödinger) do not — the latter has spectrum on the imaginary axis, and no fattened sector contains it.

Two structural consequences of analyticity, both pivotal for parabolic PDEs:

  • Instant smoothing. For $t>0$ and any $k\ge 0$: $T(t)x\in D(A^k)$ for every $x\in X$, and $\|A^k T(t)\|\le C_k/t^k$. Apply this with $A=\Delta$: $T(t)L^2\subset H^{2k}$ for every $k$, so $T(t)L^2\subset C^\infty$ for every $t>0$. The heat equation regularizes data instantly.
  • Maximal $L^p$ regularity. If $A$ generates an analytic semigroup on a UMD space (a Banach space where the Hilbert transform is bounded — includes every $L^p$ with $1<p<\infty$), the inhomogeneous problem $u'-Au=f$ with $u(0)=0$ has a solution with $u', Au\in L^p(0,T;X)$ whenever $f\in L^p(0,T;X)$, with norm equivalent to $\|f\|$. This is the right $L^p$-existence theory for parabolic PDEs.

Comparison: the wave-equation propagator on $H^1\times L^2$ is a $C_0$-group with $\|T(t)\|=1$ (energy conservation) but not analytic — initial singularities propagate forever, never smoothing. The Schrödinger group $e^{-it\Delta}$ has the same behaviour: singularities disperse but the wavefront set (the phase-space record of singular directions) is preserved, no instant smoothing.

(function(){
  const svg = document.getElementById('sg-an-svg');
  const out = document.getElementById('sg-an-out');
  const tS = document.getElementById('sg-an-t');
  const tO = document.getElementById('sg-an-t-out');
  const bH = document.getElementById('sg-an-heat');
  const bW = document.getElementById('sg-an-wave');
  const bQ = document.getElementById('sg-an-schro');
  let kind = 'heat';
  function setH(){ kind='heat'; bH.classList.add('active'); bW.classList.remove('active'); bQ.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  function setW(){ kind='wave'; bW.classList.add('active'); bH.classList.remove('active'); bQ.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  function setQ(){ kind='schro'; bQ.classList.add('active'); bH.classList.remove('active'); bW.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  const N = 220;
  const xs = [];
  for(let k=0;k<N;k++) xs.push(-Math.PI + (2*Math.PI*k)/(N-1));
  function erf(x){
    const t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911*Math.abs(x));
    const y = 1 - (((((1.061405429*t - 1.453152027)*t) + 1.421413741)*t - 0.284496736)*t + 0.254829592)*t * Math.exp(-x*x);
    return x < 0 ? -y : y;
  }
  function step(x){ return 0.5 * (1 + erf(8*x)); }
  // Smooth periodic bump for the dispersive case: tanh-flat between +-pi, smoothly fading to 0 by x = +-pi/2 outside the bump.
  // bump(x) = sigmoid-localized rising edge that vanishes near +-pi to avoid Gibbs in periodic Fourier extension.
  function bump(x){
    // 0.5*(tanh(8x) - tanh(8(x - pi/2))*0)  -- simpler: use a 2pi-periodic smooth function with a narrow rising-edge in [-pi/2, pi/2] that is zero at +-pi.
    // Choose: 0.5*(1+erf(8x)) * window(x), with window vanishing smoothly at +-pi.
    const w = Math.exp(-Math.pow(x/1.4, 8));
    return 0.5*(1 + erf(8*x)) * w;
  }
  function applyT(t){
    if(kind === 'heat'){
      // For u0 = step(x) = 0.5*(1+erf(alpha x)) with alpha=8, heat solution is 0.5*(1+erf(alpha x / sqrt(1+4 alpha^2 t))) = 0.5*(1+erf(8 x / sqrt(1+256 t))).
      const denom = Math.sqrt(1 + 256*t);
      return xs.map(x => 0.5*(1 + erf(8*x/denom)));
    }

    }
    // Schrodinger: use a SMOOTH 2pi-periodic test function (bump) so periodic Fourier expansion is not corrupted by edge Gibbs.
    const K = 60;
    const ck = [];
    for(let k=-K;k<=K;k++){
      let re = 0, im = 0;

        const c = Math.cos(phase), si = Math.sin(phase);

    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const t = +tS.value;
    tO.textContent = `t = ${t.toFixed(3)}`;
    const xL = -240, xR = 240, yMid = 30;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL,y1:yMid,x2:xR,y2:yMid,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:0,y1:yMid-110,x2:0,y2:yMid+110,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6,'stroke-dasharray':'2 3'}));
    const X = x => x * (220/Math.PI);
    const Y = v => yMid - Math.max(-0.4, Math.min(1.4, v)) * 80;
    function plot(arr, color, dash){
      let d = '';
      for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
        const px = X(xs[k]), py = Y(arr[k]);
        d += (k===0 ? 'M' : 'L') + ` ${px.toFixed(1)} ${py.toFixed(1)} `;
      }
      const p = SVG('path',{d, fill:'none', stroke:color, 'stroke-width':1.5});
      if(dash) p.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', dash);
      svg.appendChild(p);
    }
    plot(applyT(0), 'var(--mute)', '3 3');
    plot(applyT(t), kind==='heat' ? 'var(--cyan)' : kind==='wave' ? 'var(--yellow)' : 'var(--violet)', null);
    const desc = SVG('text',{x:0, y:-128, 'text-anchor':'middle', 'font-size':11, fill:'var(--ink)'});
    desc.textContent = kind === 'heat'
      ? `Heat: edge thickness widens like sqrt(t); at any t > 0, u(t,x) is C-infinity (analytic semigroup, instant smoothing).`
      : kind === 'wave'
      ? `Wave: edge splits into two pulses moving at +-1; sharpness preserved exactly (finite speed, no smoothing).`
      : `Schroedinger (smooth periodic bump): high modes spin at rate k^2, dispersive but no instant smoothing.`;
    svg.appendChild(desc);
    let maxSlope = 0;
    const ut = applyT(t);
    for(let k=1;k<ut.length;k++){
      maxSlope = Math.max(maxSlope, Math.abs(ut[k]-ut[k-1])/(xs[k]-xs[k-1]+1e-9));
    }
    out.textContent = `${kind === 'heat' ? 'Heat (analytic)' : kind === 'wave' ? 'Wave (hyperbolic)' : 'Schroedinger (dispersive)'}: t = ${t.toFixed(3)}, max-slope of u(t,x) approx ${maxSlope.toFixed(2)}.

'DROPS like 1/sqrt(t) (analyticity, T(t) maps L^2 into H^k for every k)' : kind === 'wave' ? 'STAYS constant - finite speed of propagation; the conormal of the edge propagates forever' : 'OSCILLATES - high-mode dispersion produces ringing but no L^2 smoothing'}.

  }

  bQ.addEventListener('click', setQ);
  tS.addEventListener('input', draw);
  draw();

5. Evolution equations as abstract Cauchy problems

Recast a linear PDE in evolutionary form by choosing a Banach space $X$ and a generator $A$ on $X$ so the equation becomes

$$u'(t)\;=\;A\,u(t)\;+\;f(t),\qquad u(0)\;=\;u_0,\qquad t\in[0,T].$$

This is the abstract Cauchy problem. The benefit is uniformity: every linear time-evolution PDE in this notebook fits the same template, with $X$ and $A$ chosen to fit the equation. Heat: $X=L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $A=\Delta$, $D(A)=H^2$. Wave (first-order form): $X=H^1\times L^2$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\\Delta&0\end{pmatrix}$. Schrödinger: $X=L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $A=-i\Delta$. Advection-diffusion: $X=L^2$, $A=\Delta-b\cdot\nabla$, $D(A)=H^2$.

Two notions of solution are useful. A strict (classical) solution on $[0,T]$ is $u\in C^1([0,T];X)\cap C([0,T];D(A))$ satisfying the equation pointwise. A mild solution is the integrated form: by the variation-of-parameters / Duhamel formula,

$$u(t) \;=\; T(t)\,u_0 \;+\; \int_0^t T(t-s)\,f(s)\,ds.$$

If $A$ generates a $C_0$-semigroup $T$, the homogeneous part contributes $T(t)u_0$ for any $u_0\in X$ (continuous in $t$, classical only when $u_0\in D(A)$); the inhomogeneous part demands an integrability condition on $f$. Standard sufficient conditions: $f\in C([0,T];X)$ + $u_0\in D(A)$ gives a mild solution that is automatically continuous; $f\in C^1$ or $f\in C([0,T];D(A))$ promotes mild → classical. The mild form is the right generality: it gives existence under minimum hypotheses, and the classical regularity then follows from extra conditions on $f$.

Uniqueness is automatic given $A$ closed (generators of $C_0$-semigroups are): two mild solutions differ by an orbit of the homogeneous problem starting at zero, which is identically zero by the semigroup law. The result: once $A$ generates a $C_0$-semigroup, the abstract Cauchy problem $u'=Au+f$ with $u(0)=u_0$ has a unique mild solution for every $u_0\in X$ and every continuous $f$, given by Duhamel's formula.

  function setPulse(){ kind='fpulse'; bPulse.classList.add('active'); bNone.classList.remove('active'); bConst.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  function setConst(){ kind='fconst'; bConst.classList.add('active'); bNone.classList.remove('active'); bPulse.classList.remove('active'); draw(); }
  const N = 220;
  const xs = [];
  for(let k=0;k<N;k++) xs.push(-Math.PI + (2*Math.PI*k)/(N-1));
  function u0(x){ return Math.exp(-3*x*x); }
  function g(x){ return Math.exp(-4*(x-1)*(x-1)); }
  function Tt(t, fn, var0){
    if(t < 1e-6) return xs.map(fn);
    const sigma2 = var0 + 2*t;
    const amp = Math.sqrt(var0/sigma2);
    if(fn === u0){
      return xs.map(x => amp * Math.exp(-x*x/(2*sigma2)));
    }
    return xs.map(x => amp * Math.exp(-(x-1)*(x-1)/(2*sigma2)));
  }
  function Th_u0(t){ return Tt(t, u0, 1/6); }
  function Th_g(t){ return Tt(t, g, 1/8); }
  function draw(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const t = +tS.value;
    tO.textContent = `t = ${t.toFixed(2)}`;
    const xL = -240, xR = 240;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL,y1:0,x2:xR,y2:0,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:0,y1:-120,x2:0,y2:120,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6,'stroke-dasharray':'2 3'}));
    const X = x => x * (220/Math.PI);
    const Y = v => -Math.max(0, Math.min(1.4, v)) * 80;
    function plot(arr, color, dash){
      let d = '';
      for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
        const px = X(xs[k]), py = Y(arr[k]);
        d += (k===0 ? 'M' : 'L') + ` ${px.toFixed(1)} ${py.toFixed(1)} `;
      }
      const p = SVG('path',{d, fill:'none', stroke:color, 'stroke-width':1.6});
      if(dash) p.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', dash);
      svg.appendChild(p);
    }
    const homo = Th_u0(t);
    plot(homo, 'var(--cyan)', null);
    let inhomo = xs.map(_ => 0);
    if(kind === 'fpulse'){
      if(t > 0.2){
        inhomo = Th_g(t-0.2);
      }
    } else if(kind === 'fconst'){
      const M = 24;
      for(let m=0;m<M;m++){
        const s = (m+0.5)*t/M;
        const Tg = Th_g(t-s);
        for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++) inhomo[k] += Tg[k] * (t/M);
      }
    }
    if(kind !== 'fno') plot(inhomo, 'var(--yellow)', null);
    const total = homo.map((v,i) => v + inhomo[i]);
    plot(total, 'var(--violet)', '3 3');
    const lg = (x, y, c, txt, dash) => {
      const ln = SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:y,x2:x+18,y2:y,stroke:c,'stroke-width':2});
      if(dash) ln.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', dash);
      svg.appendChild(ln);
      const t = SVG('text',{x:x+24,y:y+3,'font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent = txt; svg.appendChild(t);
    };
    lg(-235, -130, 'var(--cyan)', 'T(t) u0 (homogeneous)');
    if(kind !== 'fno') lg(-90, -130, 'var(--yellow)', 'integral T(t-s) f(s) ds (Duhamel)');
    lg(140, -130, 'var(--violet)', 'u(t) = total', '3 3');
    out.textContent = `Forcing: ${kind === 'fno' ? 'f = 0 (pure semigroup orbit)' : kind === 'fpulse' ? 'f = delta(s-0.2) g (impulse)' : 'f = g (constant-in-time)'}    t = ${t.toFixed(2)}.
Duhamel: u(t) = T(t) u0 + integral_0^t T(t-s) f(s) ds. Homogeneous part is the same in all three cases (cyan); yellow shows the convolution-against-the-semigroup contribution; violet is their sum.
${kind === 'fpulse' && t > 0.2 ? `Pulse already fired at s=0.2 (delta s = ${(t-0.2).toFixed(2)} ago); contribution is T(${(t-0.2).toFixed(2)}) g - Gaussian widened by 2(t-0.2).` : kind === 'fpulse' ? 'Pulse fires at s=0.2; for t < 0.2 the integral is empty (causality).' : kind === 'fconst' ? `Constant forcing accumulates; the integrand at small s is more spread (ran longer through T) than at s near t.` : 'Pure orbit; widening by 2t in the variance.'}`;
  }
  bNone.addEventListener('click', setNone);
  bPulse.addEventListener('click', setPulse);
  bConst.addEventListener('click', setConst);
  tS.addEventListener('input', draw);
  draw();
})();
</script>

6. Applications: nonlinear PDEs, control, and stochastic flows

Three downstream uses of the semigroup framework — each uses Duhamel's formula plus an extra ingredient.

(a) Nonlinear PDEs by fixed-point iteration. Consider $u'=Au+F(u)$, $u(0)=u_0$, with $A$ generating a $C_0$-semigroup and $F\colon X\to X$ locally Lipschitz. The Duhamel form

$$u(t)\;=\;T(t)u_0\;+\;\int_0^t T(t-s)F(u(s))\,ds$$

turns the equation into a fixed-point problem $u=\Phi(u)$ on $C([0,T_*];X)$. For $T_*$ small, $\Phi$ is a contraction (Lipschitz constant of $F$ times $T_*\sup_t\|T(t)\|$); Banach's theorem gives a unique mild solution on $[0,T_*]$. The maximal interval of existence is determined by a blow-up criterion: either the solution exists for all $t\ge 0$, or $\limsup_{t\to T_{\max}}\|u(t)\|=\infty$. This recipe handles semilinear heat ($A=\Delta$, $F=u^p$ — Fujita's theorem on critical exponents), Navier–Stokes (mild solutions of Kato), reaction-diffusion, and nonlinear Schrödinger.

(b) Control theory. The controlled system $u'=Au+Bv$, $u(0)=u_0$, with $B$ a control operator and $v(t)$ the control input, has $u(T)=T(T)u_0+\int_0^T T(T-s)Bv(s)\,ds$. Approximate controllability from $u_0$ at time $T$: the reachable set $\{T(T)u_0+\int_0^T T(T-s)Bv\,ds:v\in L^2(0,T;U)\}$ is dense in $X$. Exact controllability: it equals $X$. For the heat equation on a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ with control on a subdomain $\omega\subset\Omega$, $\omega$ open and nonempty, the system is approximately controllable in any time $T>0$ — a consequence of analyticity (controllability inherits from the Hahn–Banach dual problem about unique continuation, which holds for analytic semigroups). For wave equations, exact controllability requires $\omega$ to satisfy the geometric control condition: every billiard trajectory must enter $\omega$ in finite time (Bardos–Lebeau–Rauch).

(c) Stochastic flows. An Itô SDE $dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t)\,dW_t$ with smooth $b,\sigma$ defines the Markov semigroup $T(t)f(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(X_t)\mid X_0=x]$ on bounded measurable functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Itô's formula computes its generator: at smooth $f$,

$$Af(x)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^\top)_{ij}(x)\,\partial_i\partial_j f(x)\;+\;\sum_i b_i(x)\,\partial_i f(x).$$

This is a second-order elliptic operator (degenerate when $\sigma\sigma^\top$ is rank-deficient). For $\sigma=I$ and $b=0$ — Brownian motion — $A=\frac{1}{2}\Delta$, recovering the heat semigroup. The link is the Feynman–Kac formula: solutions of parabolic PDEs $u_t=Au+Vu$ have stochastic representations $u(t,x)=\mathbb{E}_x[e^{\int_0^t V(X_s)ds}f(X_t)]$, turning analytic estimates on $T(t)$ into probabilistic statements about path integrals (and vice versa).

params.bodyScript:
<script>
(function(){
  const svg = document.getElementById('sg-ctl-svg');
  const out = document.getElementById('sg-ctl-out');
  const wS = document.getElementById('sg-ctl-w');
  const rS = document.getElementById('sg-ctl-r');
  const TS = document.getElementById('sg-ctl-T');
  const wO = document.getElementById('sg-ctl-w-out');
  const rO = document.getElementById('sg-ctl-r-out');
  const TO = document.getElementById('sg-ctl-T-out');
  const N = 80;
  const xs = [];
  for(let k=0;k<N;k++) xs.push(-Math.PI + (2*Math.PI*k)/(N-1));
  const dx = xs[1] - xs[0];
  function u0Fn(x){ return Math.exp(-3*x*x); }
  function uTFn(x){ return 0.5 * Math.exp(-3*(x-1)*(x-1)); }
  function Tu0(T){
    const sigma2 = 1/6 + 2*T;
    const amp = Math.sqrt((1/6)/sigma2);
    return xs.map(x => amp * Math.exp(-x*x/(2*sigma2)));
  }
  function indicator(x, w, r){ return (Math.abs(x-w) < r) ? 1 : 0; }
  // Naive controlled trajectory: u_ctrl(T,x) = T(T)u0 + 1_omega(x) * (u_T(x) - T(T)u0(x)) -- the simplest projection-onto-omega control.
  // Residual on omega^c = (u_T - T(T)u0) restricted to omega^c is what cannot be matched by such a naive controller.
  function controlled(T, w, r){
    const drift = Tu0(T);
    return xs.map((x, k) => {
      const inOmega = indicator(x, w, r);
      return drift[k] + inOmega * (uTFn(x) - drift[k]);
    });
  }
  function controlCost(T, w, r){
    const drift = Tu0(T);
    let targetSq = 0, missedSq = 0, areaW = 0;
    // Centroid distance of omega from the target's mass center (target is centered near x=1)
    let targetCenter = 0, targetMass = 0;
    for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
      const v = uTFn(xs[k]);
      targetCenter += xs[k] * v * dx;
      targetMass += v * dx;
    }
    const xT = targetMass > 1e-9 ? targetCenter/targetMass : 0;
    const distOmegaToTarget = Math.abs(w - xT);
    for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
      const dif = uTFn(xs[k]) - drift[k];
      targetSq += dif*dif * dx;
      const inOmega = indicator(xs[k], w, r);
      areaW += inOmega * dx;
      if(!inOmega) missedSq += dif*dif * dx;
    }
    const target = Math.sqrt(targetSq);
    const unreachable = Math.sqrt(missedSq);
    // LQR-style cost: grows with target norm, e^{c/T}, and 1/sqrt(area). Add a penalty (1 + |w - x_target|) so that
    // moving the window AWAY from the target's center increases cost - now w is a real control knob, not just decorative.
    const Tcost = areaW > 0 ? Math.exp(1.0/Math.max(T, 0.05)) * target * (1 + distOmegaToTarget) / Math.sqrt(areaW) : Infinity;
    const ratio = target > 1e-9 ? unreachable / target : 0;
    return { target, missed: unreachable, areaW, cost: Tcost, ratio, distOmegaToTarget };
  }
  function draw(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const w = +wS.value, r = +rS.value, T = +TS.value;
    wO.textContent = `x_omega = ${w.toFixed(2)}`;
    rO.textContent = `radius = ${r.toFixed(2)}`;
    TO.textContent = `T = ${T.toFixed(2)}`;
    const xL = -240, xR = 240, yMid = 30;
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:xL,y1:yMid,x2:xR,y2:yMid,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:0,y1:yMid-110,x2:0,y2:yMid+110,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':0.6,'stroke-dasharray':'2 3'}));
    const X = x => x * (220/Math.PI);
    const Y = v => yMid - Math.max(0, Math.min(1.4, v)) * 80;
    function plot(yfn, color, dash, width){
      let d = '';
      for(let k=0;k<xs.length;k++){
        const px = X(xs[k]), py = yfn(xs[k], k);
        d += (k===0 ? 'M' : 'L') + ` ${px.toFixed(1)} ${py.toFixed(1)} `;
      }
      const p = SVG('path',{d, fill:'none', stroke:color, 'stroke-width':width||1.6});
      if(dash) p.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', dash);
      svg.appendChild(p);
    }
    const wL = Math.max(-Math.PI, w - r), wR = Math.min(Math.PI, w + r);
    svg.appendChild(SVG('rect',{x:X(wL), y:yMid-90, width:X(wR)-X(wL), height:180, fill:'var(--green)', opacity:0.12, stroke:'var(--green)','stroke-width':1}));
    plot(x => Y(u0Fn(x)), 'var(--mute)', '3 3');
    plot(x => Y(uTFn(x)), 'var(--yellow)', null);
    const drift = Tu0(T);
    plot((x, k) => Y(drift[k]), 'var(--cyan)', '2 2');
    const ctrl = controlled(T, w, r);
    plot((x, k) => Y(ctrl[k]), 'var(--violet)', null, 2.0);
    const lg = (x, y, c, txt, dash) => {
      const ln = SVG('line',{x1:x,y1:y,x2:x+18,y2:y,stroke:c,'stroke-width':2});
      if(dash) ln.setAttribute('stroke-dasharray', dash);
      svg.appendChild(ln);
      const t = SVG('text',{x:x+24,y:y+3,'font-size':10,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent = txt; svg.appendChild(t);
    };
    lg(-235, -130, 'var(--mute)', 'u0', '3 3');
    lg(-200, -118, 'var(--cyan)', 'T(T) u0 (drift)', '2 2');
    lg(-105, -130, 'var(--yellow)', 'target u_T');
    lg(-30, -118, 'var(--violet)', 'controlled u(T,x) (naive proj)');
    const omegaText = SVG('text',{x:140, y:-130, 'font-size':10, fill:'var(--green)'}); omegaText.textContent = 'omega (control)'; svg.appendChild(omegaText);
    const c = controlCost(T, w, r);
    out.textContent = `Heat equation u_t = u_xx on [-pi, pi], control window omega = [${w.toFixed(2)} +- ${r.toFixed(2)}], horizon T = ${T.toFixed(2)}.
Drift T(T) u0 vs target u_T: |u_T - T(T) u0|_{L^2} approx ${c.target.toFixed(3)} (residual the control must close).
Naive projection-onto-omega controller (violet) matches the target inside omega and falls back to the drift outside; residual outside omega: |u_T - T(T)u0|_{L^2(omega^c)} approx ${c.missed.toFixed(3)} (= ${(c.ratio*100).toFixed(1)}% of total residual not corrected by this controller).
Approximate controllability (analytic-semigroup theory) says a TRUE control closes the residual to any precision; the cost grows like e^{c/T} for small T. Cost estimate (with omega-to-target distance ${c.distOmegaToTarget.toFixed(2)}): |v|_{L^2(0,T;omega)} approx ${c.cost.toFixed(2)} - moving omega away from the target's center makes the cost worse.
Approximate is not exact: for parabolic eqs the reachable set is dense but not all of L^2 (instant smoothing means u(T) lies in intersection_k H^k). The exponential blow-up e^{c/T} is the observability cost (Lebeau-Robbiano: short horizons need exponentially expensive controls).`;
  }
  wS.addEventListener('input', draw);
  rS.addEventListener('input', draw);
  TS.addEventListener('input', draw);
  draw();
})();
</script>

7. Connections

Semigroup theory is the operator-theoretic spine that makes "evolution PDE" a single subject rather than a list of equations. Open frontiers include nonautonomous (time-dependent generators $A(t)$) and the corresponding evolution families, semigroups on quasi-Banach / Fréchet spaces (kinetic / Boltzmann theory), the link between dispersive and parabolic regularity (smoothing estimates for Schrödinger), and the analytic-semigroup theory of stochastic PDEs (Da Prato–Zabczyk's mild-solution machine for $du = A u\,dt + dW$).

  • Functional analysis — Bounded operators & adjoints — the Banach-space scaffolding that holds $T(t)$ and $A$.
  • Partial differential equations — Heat equation & heat kernel — the canonical analytic-semigroup example, fully visible at the level of the Gaussian kernel.
  • Sobolev spaces & distributions — $W^{k,p}$ and $H^s$ — the natural domains $D(A^k)$ for differential generators.
  • Spectral theory — spectrum of a self-adjoint operator — diagonalizes self-adjoint generators so $T(t)=e^{tA}$ is computed mode-by-mode.
  • Microlocal analysis — wavefront set — explains why Schrödinger and wave propagators preserve singularities (no instant smoothing) while heat erases them.
  • Stochastic calculus — Itô formula — derives the second-order elliptic generator of a Markov semigroup from an SDE.
  • Stochastic processes & martingales — continuous martingales — Markov semigroup acts on bounded measurable functions of the diffusion's path.
